context: Adh-Dhariyat is Makkan, and it settles its subject in the first six verses: what you are promised is true, and the recompense is going to occur. Everything after that is evidence, drawn from the sky and the earth, the nightly habits of the righteous, the guests who came to Ibrahim, and the wreckage left by four earlier nations.

What it leaves out marks it as Makkan: no law, no organising of a community, no address to hypocrites. What it supplies instead answers two questions a harassed minority would have been asking, when the Day of Recompense is, asked mockingly in verse 12, and where provision comes from, answered in verse 22 and again at the close.
name_story: The name comes from the first word of the first verse, adh-dhariyat, the winds that scatter dust. The four opening oaths are usually read as a sequence of winds, clouds, ships and angels, though the early commentators differed over which is meant by each. The surah is therefore named for something invisible whose effects are not.

movements.note: Four oaths in four short verses land on one statement, that the recompense will occur. Those who ask mockingly when that Day is are shown held over the Fire, told to taste what they were impatient for.

movements.h: The righteous, and where provision comes from
movements.note: The people of the gardens are described by their nights: they slept little, sought forgiveness before dawn, and kept a share of their wealth for the one who asked and the one too restrained to ask.

Guests arrive, a fattened calf is brought, and their hands do not reach for it. Ibrahim conceals his fear, they give news of a knowing son, his wife strikes her face and calls herself barren, and they go on to Lut's people.
Musa is sent to Fir'awn, who turns away and says magician or madman. 'Ad is given a barren wind, Thamud is seized by a thunderbolt, and the people of Nuh are dealt with in one verse.

Three statements about creation follow one another, each a clause long, ending with the note that everything was made in pairs. Then comes the imperative the surah has been moving toward, to flee to Allah.
Earlier peoples said of their messengers exactly what Quraysh said of the Prophet ﷺ, magician or madman, and the surah closes by naming why jinn and mankind were created.

themes.t: Provision is not the reader's to arrange
themes.d: Verse 22 and verse 58 place sustenance entirely on Allah's side, inside a surah about the Day of Recompense. Worry about income is set beside doubt about the Hereafter, not treated separately.

themes.t: The purpose stated once and plainly
themes.d: Verse 56 gives the reason jinn and mankind exist in a single sentence, and its placement carries part of the meaning, since it arrives after a surah's worth of material about food, guests, wealth and rain.

Ibrahim's conduct with the guests is reported as a sequence of actions: he slips away to his family, returns with a fattened calf, brings it near. No verse commends him, and the reporting is the commendation.

Verse 52 observes that every earlier people used the same two words about their messenger. Since they were separated by centuries and could not have arranged it, the charge becomes evidence about the accusers.

heart: This surah rewards being read once out of order and then in order. Verses 15 to 19 describe the righteous entirely through habits: how much of the night they slept, when they sought forgiveness, what they set aside for those who asked and for those who never did. Nothing is said of what they felt, which makes the passage unusually testable against a reader's own week.

The other place that changes on slow reading is the command in verse 50, to flee to Allah. Flight assumes something fled from, and the verse does not name it. Coming after the built sky and the spread earth, it leaves a reader to notice that the only refuge named is the One whose punishment is escaped.

passages.why: The righteous described by their nights and their giving, concrete enough to check a life against rather than admire.
Provision placed in the heaven alongside what has been promised, one short verse that reframes an anxiety most readers carry daily.
The single imperative the surah builds toward, worth returning to for what it leaves unstated about the direction of the danger.
The stated purpose of the creation of jinn and mankind, read in place at the end of a surah about rain and wealth, not as a slogan.

connections.why: Hud tells the visit to Ibrahim and the destruction of Lut's people at length, with the dialogue Adh-Dhariyat leaves out. The compressed version is easier to hold; the long one explains it.
Al-Mursalat also opens with oaths by winds and drives toward the recompense, but works by refrain: one opening device put to two uses.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Adh-Dhariyat. Reports circulating in later works that assign a named reward to each surah in turn were judged fabricated by the hadith critics, and nothing sound has been established for this one. Its standing rests on its content, above all verse 56, among the most cited verses in the Qur'an on why human beings exist.
